notes.b: A competition needs more than one person keeping order. Different officials look after different jobs, and the type you meet depends on the activity.
points: The referee or umpire is in charge of the contest. They apply the rules and make the final decisions on play, so every other official ultimately supports them.

A linesperson or assistant referee judges line calls (for example, whether a ball is in or out) or helps the referee with positions such as offside, because the referee cannot watch the whole pitch at once.
Umpires in Gaelic games are positioned around the field to watch their own area, help the referee and signal scores to the scorers.
Judges in gymnastics, diving and dance score routines and performances against set criteria, because these activities are not won by a clock or a goal.
Timekeepers keep the official time, and scorers record the scores and results, so the outcome is accurate and agreed.
Starters in athletics and swimming start the race, which makes sure every competitor begins at the same moment.
Video officials, such as the television match official (TMO) in rugby, review contested decisions using video footage.
notes.tip: When asked to outline the roles of two competition officials, pick two different types, such as a referee and a timekeeper or judge, and give each one's job in a named activity.

notes.b: Whatever the activity, officials share a set of core jobs. Together they make the contest fair, safe and properly recorded.
points: Apply and interpret the rules throughout the contest, so that both sides are treated by the same standard.
Keep the game flowing by restarting play promptly after each stoppage, so that time is not wasted and players stay warm and focused.
Ensure safety by stopping play when a risk appears, for example when a player is injured or equipment is faulty.
Record scores and results accurately, because the final result depends on them.
Manage discipline, using cards or sanctions (penalties) against players who break the rules.
Start and finish the contest, enforcing its time limits.
notes.tip: If asked to describe two roles of an official, give each role with what the official actually does, not just its name. For example, say that they stop play when a risk appears, which keeps players safe.

notes.b: You must be able to explain the main rules of the activities you study, covering fouls, sanctions and restarts. These examples show the pattern: what counts as a breach, what the penalty is and how play restarts.
points: Soccer: a foul such as tripping an opponent is penalised with a direct free kick, so the fouled team gets a chance to restart play with an advantage.
Soccer: after a goal, play restarts with a kick-off from the centre spot.
Basketball: a player who fouls a shooter gives the shooter free throws, which compensates the shooter for the lost scoring chance.
Basketball: after a made basket, the team that conceded inbounds the ball (puts it back into play) from behind the end line.
Tennis: a double fault, which is two consecutive faults on serve, loses the point.
Tennis: a let means the serve is replayed when the ball touches the net and lands in the correct service box.
notes.tip: Questions may ask for three rules and the scoring system of a named activity. Choose an activity you know well and cover scoring, a foul with its sanction, and a restart.

notes.h: Safety regulations and who enforces them
notes.b: Each activity has its own safety regulations, and a specific official is responsible for enforcing each one. Knowing both the rule and the person who enforces it is what the exam asks for.
points: The referee checks for jewellery and studs before play, because these can cut or injure other players.
A lifeguard or official enforces pool depth rules and bans diving in shallow water, because hitting the bottom can cause serious injury.
A high-jump official checks that the landing mats are in place and correctly positioned, so jumpers land on a cushioned surface.
A hurling referee enforces the requirement to wear helmets with faceguards, which protect the head and face from the ball and the hurley.
notes.tip: For each activity you are asked about, give one safety regulation and name the official who implements it. Do not give the rule without the official.

notes.b: Before a contest begins, officials check equipment, facilities and player clothing so that hazards are removed in advance. This subsection covers the official's checks.
points: Equipment: balls are correctly inflated, because a ball that is too hard or soft behaves unpredictably, and posts and nets are secure, with padding on posts where required.
Facilities: the playing surface is free of glass, holes and debris, which could cause cuts or trips.
Facilities: lines are clearly marked, lighting is adequate and run-off areas (the space around the pitch where players may slide or fall) are safe.
Player clothing: correct footwear and studs, and no jewellery, so that players do not injure themselves or others.
Player clothing: mandatory protective equipment such as helmets, gumshields and shin guards is worn.
Player clothing: kits distinguish the teams, so the officials and players can tell who is who.
notes.tip: When asked to outline two safety checks before a competition, give a precise check (such as checking the surface for glass or holes) and say what risk it prevents.

notes.h: Scoring and recording in Gaelic games
notes.b: Gaelic football and hurling use a two-level scoring system. Scorers must record goals and points separately, so the written score has a fixed format.
points: A goal, struck into the net under the crossbar, is worth 3 points.
A point, sent over the crossbar between the posts, is worth 1 point.
Scores are written as goals-points, so 2-10 means 2 goals and 10 points. In total that is 6 + 10 = 16, because each goal is worth 3.
notes.tip: If asked to outline a scoring system, state the value of each score and show how it is written, using an example such as 2-10 = 16.

notes.b: Basketball scoring depends on where the shot is taken from, so the scorer must record how each basket was made.
points: A field goal (a basket scored in open play) from inside the three-point line is worth 2 points.
A field goal from beyond the three-point line is worth 3 points, which rewards the harder, longer shot.
A free throw, awarded after certain fouls, is worth 1 point.

notes.b: Tennis does not count points one by one. Points build into games, and games build into sets, each with its own rule for who wins.
points: Points within a game are called love (zero), 15, 30, 40 and game.
At 40 all, the score is deuce. Winning the next point gives the player advantage, and winning a point from advantage wins the game.
A set is won by six games with a two-game margin, so a player cannot win a set by a single game at 6-5.
Tie-break rules vary by event.
notes.tip: Remember the sequence love, 15, 30, 40, game, then deuce and advantage. Outline tennis if you need a scoring system that differs from a points-count system like basketball.

notes.h: Scoring in athletics, swimming and judged activities
notes.b: Some activities are decided by measurement, others by the opinion of judges. You should be able to outline both methods, because exam questions ask for two activities with different systems.
points: Athletics and swimming: times and distances are recorded, because the winner is the one who is fastest or goes furthest.
Team scoring in athletics and swimming can be decided by the placing of each athlete, with points awarded for finishing position.
Gymnastics, dance and diving are judged by panels of judges, because the quality of a performance cannot be measured with a stopwatch.
Panels score difficulty and execution or artistry, so a harder routine and a cleaner or more expressive performance both earn credit.
In gymnastics, the execution score starts from a maximum, and judges deduct for each fault.
notes.tip: When asked to outline scoring for two activities with different systems, pair a measured one (such as athletics) with a judged one (such as gymnastics), and do not invent rules for unfamiliar activities.

notes.h: Demands of officiating: fitness and psychological readiness
notes.b: Officiating is demanding for both body and mind. An official who cannot keep up with play or who loses composure will make poorer decisions.
points: Cardio-respiratory endurance (the ability of heart and lungs to keep working) and speed are needed to keep up with play. For example, a rugby or soccer referee covers a large distance with repeated high-intensity efforts.
Agility and positioning: getting into the best place to see each decision, which means the official must move quickly and change direction.
Concentration for the full contest, without a lapse, because one missed incident can change the result.
Confidence and decisiveness, making calls clearly and quickly so that players accept them.
Composure (staying calm) under pressure from players, coaches and crowds.
Resilience: recovering quickly after a mistake and staying consistent, so one error does not affect later decisions.
notes.tip: To describe the demands of officiating, choose two headings, such as personal fitness and psychological readiness, and give specific demands with reasons under each.

notes.b: An official needs the right clothing and kit to do the job properly. Each item has a purpose, and you may be asked to explain why it matters.
points: Attire: a correct, distinguishable uniform, suitable footwear for the surface and weather-appropriate layers, so the official can stay comfortable and mobile.
Equipment: a whistle, with a spare in case the first fails, and a watch or stopwatch to keep time.
Equipment: a scorecard and pen to record scores and incidents, and cards: yellow, red and, where used, black.
Equipment: a coin for the toss, flags, and communication headsets at higher levels.
Importance: a coin for the toss decides the start fairly, for example which team chooses ends or who starts.
Importance: attire marks the official out and conveys authority, so players and spectators can recognise who is in charge.
notes.tip: Questions ask for the importance of two pieces of attire and two pieces of equipment in a named activity. Name the item and say why it matters, for example the spare whistle in case one fails.

notes.b: Officials must communicate their decisions so that everyone understands and accepts them. The best style is assertive: firm and clear without being hostile.
points: Assertive communication is clear, confident, firm and calm.
Decisive signals and a strong, sharp whistle show that the decision has been made, so players do not think the official is unsure.
Eye contact when making a call shows confidence and tells the player the decision is being communicated directly to them.
A brief explanation of a decision when one is needed helps players understand the call without opening a debate.
Assertive is not aggressive, such as shouting, and not passive, such as avoiding confrontation. Aggression provokes players, while passivity invites them to challenge decisions.
notes.tip: Do not describe assertive as aggressive. Say it is firm, calm and clear, and contrast it with aggressive and passive styles.

notes.h: Managing conflict between official and participants
notes.b: Players, coaches and crowds will sometimes disagree with decisions. The official's job is to keep control without turning the disagreement into an argument.
points: Stay calm and neutral, because an official who loses their temper loses authority.
Explain the decision and the rule behind it, briefly, so players know why the call was made.
Speak through the captains when a group of players protests, so the official deals with one person rather than a crowd.
Apply disciplinary sanctions consistently, so players see that the same behaviour always gets the same response.
Do not argue or debate a decision at length, because this wastes time and makes it look as though the decision can be changed.
notes.tip: Give strategies as actions, such as speaking through the captain, and say why each works. Keep this separate from conflict between players.

notes.b: Tempers can flare between players during a contest. The official's aim is to stop trouble before it grows and to keep everyone safe.
points: Separate the players quickly, before a confrontation escalates.
Intervene early and give warnings, so that minor incidents do not become serious ones.
Call the captains to calm their team-mates, because players are more likely to listen to their own leader.
Use advantage or a stoppage to cool the situation.
Apply sanctions consistently and report serious incidents, so that proper action can be taken after the contest.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to identify and describe strategies officials use for conflict between participants. Name each strategy and add how it helps, such as calling the captains to calm their team-mates.

notes.b: You are asked to evaluate your own officiating by comparing it with an official you admire, who is your own choice. The method is to judge yourself on set criteria, then turn the result into a plan.
points: Choose criteria such as positioning, decision accuracy, communication, fitness and game management.
Compare your officiating with an official you admire on each criterion, honestly, so the evaluation is useful rather than flattering.
Identify one strength and one target for development.
Set a concrete action, such as reviewing video of your own games, so that the target can actually be achieved.
notes.tip: A full evaluation has criteria, an honest comparison, one strength, one target and an action. Leave any of these out and you lose the structure.

keyTerms.definition: A person who applies the rules, keeps the contest safe and records the result.
The official in charge of a contest who applies the rules and makes the final decisions on play.
An official who judges line calls or assists the referee with positions such as offside.
The official who starts a race or swim.
An official who scores a performance against set criteria, as in gymnastics, diving or dance.
The part of a judged score that reflects how well a routine is performed, as distinct from its difficulty.
A tennis score of 40 all, after which a player must win two consecutive points to win the game.
The point won after deuce that gives a player the chance to win the game.
A formal caution shown by a referee to a player for misconduct.
Speaking clearly, confidently and calmly, and making firm decisions without being aggressive or passive.
The steps an official or participant takes to calm a dispute and stop it escalating.
A team member who represents the team with officials and speaks on its behalf.

factCards.definition: Goal: 3 points. Point: 1 point. Score written as goals-points, for example 2-10 is 16.
Two-point field goal from inside the arc, three-point field goal from beyond it, one-point free throw.

factCards.term: What a tennis set win requires
factCards.definition: Six games, with a two-game margin.
The television match official, who reviews contested decisions using video.

questions.prompt: Describe the demands of officiating in a physical activity of your choice in terms of personal fitness, psychological readiness, personal attire and equipment.
questions.model: Activity: basketball. Personal fitness: a basketball referee must keep up with a fast-moving game for the whole contest, using speed, agility and endurance to stay in position to see fouls near the ball and the basket. Psychological readiness: the referee needs concentration for the whole game, composure when players or the crowd react to a decision, and resilience to put a mistake behind them quickly. Personal attire: a referee wears a uniform that is distinct from both teams, with footwear suited to the court surface, so the official is easily identified and has grip while moving. Equipment: a whistle, which must be clear and distinct, with a spare in case of failure, a timing device to keep the game time, and the signals or cards used to show decisions.

questions.prompt: Identify and explain two strategies an official can use to manage conflict between participants.
questions.model: First, separate the players early: the official moves between them and calls the captains to calm their team-mates, so the confrontation does not escalate. Second, use an advantage or a stoppage to cool the situation, then apply sanctions consistently, warning or cautioning the player who started the incident, and report any serious incident after the contest. Both strategies work because they reduce the chance of a fight and show that the official's decisions apply equally to every player.

questions.prompt: Outline two safety checks an official should make before a competition in a physical activity of your choice.
questions.model: Activity: soccer. First, equipment: the balls are correctly inflated, and the goals are secure with any padding on the posts in place. Second, facilities: the playing surface is checked for glass, holes and debris, the lines are clearly marked and the run-off areas are safe.
